title: Distinct distances in the tetrahedral grid
statement: The tetrahedral grid of side n is the set of the n(n + 1)(n + 2)/6 points a*e1 + b*e2 + c*e3 with integers a, b, c >= 0 and a + b + c <= n - 1, where e1, e2, e3 are unit vectors at 60 degrees to each other: a tetrahedral piece of the face-centred cubic lattice, in which the squared distance between two points is da^2 + db^2 + dc^2 + da*db + db*dc + da*dc. What is the largest set of grid points whose pairwise distances are all different? For n <= 10 the answer is n (exhaustive search). The headline cell is n = 20 (1,540 points): find more than 16 points with all distances different.
submission: Text file: one line 'a b c' per point (a, b, c >= 0, a + b + c <= 19), all points distinct.
score: the number of points, an integer (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: local search that moves one point at a time to the grid point creating the fewest repeated distances, with a tabu list (tools/src/tetradist.c, mode ls)

context: Erdos's distinct distances problem asks how few distances n points can determine; its opposite, how many points can have all their distances different, is a Golomb-ruler question in higher dimensions. Erdos and Guy (1970) asked it for the n x n square grid, where the largest sets have order n^(2/3) up to logarithmic factors, and in the triangular grid (our problem tri-distinct) the answers stay below n. The face-centred cubic lattice is the densest lattice packing of spheres and the three-dimensional counterpart of the triangular lattice, and its tetrahedral pieces are the natural regions: the corners of a tetrahedron of side n - 1. Here the answer is exactly n for every n <= 10, by exhaustive search; beyond that our searches find fewer than n points (16 for n = 20), and whether the exact values stay at n for a while longer is open. Counting gives an upper bound: the squared distances are integers from 1 to (n - 1)^2, so k points need k(k - 1)/2 <= (n - 1)^2, which allows about 1.41n. Whether the largest sets grow like n, or like a larger multiple of n, is open.
references: P. Erdos, On sets of distances of n points, Amer. Math. Monthly 53 (1946) 248-250
P. Erdos, R. K. Guy, Distinct distances between lattice points, Elemente der Mathematik 25 (1970) 121-123
J. H. Conway, N. J. A. Sloane, Sphere Packings, Lattices and Groups, 3rd ed., Springer (1999) (the face-centred cubic lattice A3)
Our problem tri-distinct (distinct distances in the triangular grid)

novelty.verdict: new question for this lattice: Erdos and Guy asked it for the square grid and we for the triangular grid (tri-distinct); no result was found for the face-centred cubic lattice or its tetrahedral pieces.
closest: Our problem tri-distinct: the same question in the triangular grid (two dimensions), where the answers stay below n.
